title: The first screen of a booking product
metaTitle: The first screen of a booking product
excerpt: A booking product's first screen, for a guest on a phone and in a hurry, should show the next time they can take and one way to take it. A tour spends the only minute they have.
alt: A wide mountain valley with snowy peaks, a braided river, and evergreen trees in the foreground, a path with one obvious way forward.
caption: The way through is already in the frame. The first screen should be that direct. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a booking product show first?
faqs.answer: Show the next useful object and one action. For most guests that object is an open time, or the service they came to book with the next open time on it. The action is to choose that time. A tour, an account wall, and a gallery of the business can wait until the time is visible.

faqs.question: Should a guest create an account before they see times?
faqs.answer: Show the times first, because they are on a phone, often between two other tasks, and they came to see if a time exists. Ask for the minimum details when they commit to a slot. An account can be a consequence of the booking, not the toll before the calendar.

faqs.question: What if the business offers many services?
faqs.answer: If a link can point at one service, the first screen should be that service and its times. If they must choose, show a short list in their words, not internal package codes, and treat picking one as the action. Do not make them learn categories before they see a single bookable time.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Booking product UX on the first screen is a promise kept quickly. A guest on a phone, in a hurry, should see the next useful object and one action. Name the object. Name the action. A tour spends the only minute they brought with them.

The object is usually a time they can take, or the service they already chose with the next open time written on it. The action is to take that time. If the screen opens on a brand story, a login wall, or a carousel of rooms, they will back out and call instead. The phone call is the workaround your interface created.

## The guest is not settling in

They are in a car park, a hallway, or the gap between two meetings. Someone sent a link. The link is the whole relationship so far. The first screen has to honor the link.

If the link was for a specific service, that service is already chosen. Show its name in their words, the length, the place or the call link, and the next times. If the link was for a specific person on the team, that person is chosen. Do not make them re-pick what the link already knew.

Jakob Nielsen, for the Nielsen Norman Group, wrote that people often leave a web page in 10 to 20 seconds, and that a clear value proposition in the first 10 seconds is what earns a longer look. For this guest, the value proposition is a real time they can still get. [How long people stay on a page](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is the research to cite when a stakeholder wants a welcome modal before the calendar.

Hurry changes the layout. The first view on a phone should contain the service name and at least one tappable time, without scrolling past a photograph. The photograph can exist. It cannot push the time below the fold. A beautiful header that hides the calendar is a poster, not a booking.

## Name the object out loud

Use the words the guest used when they asked for the link. Intro call. Haircut. Table for two. Site visit. If your admin tool calls it SKU-14 or "Tier B consult," that name stays in the admin tool. The guest screen uses the public name, the duration, and the price if the price is something they will ask about anyway.

Show the next useful times, not a month of emptiness. The next three open slots, with the day written in words, beat a calendar grid that starts on a week you cannot book. A grid can be the way to look further. It should not be the only way to see that tomorrow at 9 is open.

Put the timezone in the same view as the times. A guest in a hurry will book the wrong hour and blame you, correctly, if the zone was a footnote. Default to the zone their phone is in, say the zone in text, and let them change it without leaving the screen. The change should update the times in place.

One noun, all the way through. If the button says "Choose Tuesday at 9:00," the confirmation should say they chose Tuesday at 9:00. "Submit reservation" is a different product. The guest did not come to submit. They came to take a time.

If nothing is open soon, the object is that fact. "The next intro call is Thursday" is a useful object. A disabled calendar with no sentence is not. Offer the first real time and a way to ask for another day. Do not pretend the week is bookable when it is not.

## One action, in the thumb's reach

The action is Choose this time. Place it on the time itself. A time that is text, followed by a separate Continue somewhere else, makes them hold a slot in their head. Tapping the time should select it and show the single next step.

The next step is the minimum you need to hold the slot. A name and a way to reach them is often enough. Payment, if you must take it now, comes after the time is obvious, with the time still on screen. Asking for a password, a profile photo, and a marketing opt-in before the time is confirmed is how you lose a guest who was ready.

Do not offer a second equal action. "Learn more" beside "Book" splits the thumb. If they need a fact to decide, put the fact on the screen: where it is, how long it is, what to bring. A link to a long policy can sit under those facts. It is not the action.

Account creation can ride along after the booking exists. "We made an account so you can change this time" is a consequence they understand. "Create an account to see the calendar" is a toll. They will not pay it on a phone in a hurry. They will screenshot your Instagram and send a message instead.

If a slot can disappear while they look, say what happens when they tap. Either you hold it for the length of the form, and you say so, or you do not hold it, and you say you will tell them if it goes. Silence here becomes the error article's problem. The first screen can prevent that surprise by being honest about the hold.

## What a tour costs on a phone

A tour on this screen is any sequence that delays the first time. A splash. A coach mark on the menu. A slide about the story of the studio. A cookie wall that covers the calendar, if you can avoid covering it. The guest did not arrive to be oriented. They arrived to leave with a time.

Count the taps from the opened link to a visible open slot. The number should be zero or one. One is acceptable when they must pick a service the link did not specify. Two is a leak. Three is a different product, usually a marketing site that happens to contain a booking widget at the bottom.

If the marketing site and the booking are the same URL, the first screen of the booking still has to be reachable in one tap from the line they tapped in the email or the bio. Do not drop them on a homepage and trust them to find Schedule. The link should open the object.

Motion before the times load is the same delay. Prefer a stable layout with the service name already there and the times filling in. A skeleton in the shape of the time list is fine. A full-screen animation is not. People who prefer reduced motion should get the times with no ceremony. So should everyone else on this screen. Hurry is its own reduced-motion case.

## What to leave off the first view

Leave the staff directory off, unless they must choose a person and the link did not choose one. Leave reviews, a map, and a gallery under the times, not above them. Those support trust after the object is visible. Above the object, they are obstacles.

Leave the full policy off. One line on cancellation belongs near the action if it would change the decision. "You can change this time until the day before" is that kind of line. A PDF is not.

Leave social login off the first view. It is a fine option on the step where you ask for an email. It is a strange first impression when they have not yet seen a time.

Leave upsells off until the time is held. A hurried guest who is offered a longer service, a product, and a newsletter before they have a slot will feel processed. Add one relevant extra after the slot is clear, or on the confirmation. Not before.

If you are tempted to explain how the calendar works, the calendar is too clever. A list of real times needs almost no explanation. A grid with colors, icons, and a legend needs a manual. Choose the list for the first view. Offer the grid as a way to jump ahead.

## Review it the way the guest will meet it

Open the public link on a phone, on a cellular connection, in a private window so you are not already signed in as the owner. You should see a named service and a real time without scrolling. You should be able to say the timezone. You should reach a confirmation without creating a password first.

Try a link with no availability in the next few days. The screen should name the next real time. Try a link that points at a service you have since renamed in the admin. The public name should be the one in the email you sent, or you should stop sending the old name.

Then make the booking fail on purpose. The slot gets taken. The card is declined. The next piece is [errors in a booking product](/blog/errors-in-a-booking-product). A first screen that only demos with an empty test calendar is not done. The guest in a hurry will meet the failure, and they will not wait for your illustration to load.

When the first screen of a product should be this direct, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The work is the object, the action, and the sentence that keeps a hurried person oriented. The rest can follow after they have a time.
